title: Claude + Three.js = Premium 3D Motion Graphics
summary: A demo-led tutorial on making 3D motion graphics entirely as code. Claude writes a Three.js scene with GPU shaders, the scene renders in a headless browser, and frames are captured at 60fps and stitched into video. No AI video model or After Effects is involved. The creator walks through five demos: a glassmorphic particle scene, metallic reflective spheres, a 3D RAG/vector explainer, a paper-textured gradient-descent explainer, and a globe showing packet routing. His prompting tips are: write a scene-by-scene spec with timings; name Three.js and shaders explicitly; ask for camera moves through 3D space and motion within each scene; ask for 'professional and sleek'; use a 'job-application showreel' role-play framing; let a strong model propose three ideas before building; and run a verification loop for overlapping elements and too-small text. He claims Opus 5.5 is clearly the best model for this. He prices a 15-second clip at about 5 cents on a Claude subscription, against roughly $1.50 on Seedance 2.5, where every revision is paid again. Use cases he names are social short-form, explainers, product launches, and overlays on podcast or client-call clips. The video ends with a pitch for his paid mastermind.
recencySignals: Names Opus 5.5 as the current best model, and also mentions 'Sonnet 5.5', 'Astra 6' and Seedance 2.5 as one of the best current video models. He says the results were impossible 'a couple of months ago'. HyperFrames and Remotion are referenced as alternatives. These cues place it in the second half of 2026, close to today (2026-11-12), so the platform-mechanics claims are fresh.

tactics.claim: Build motion graphics as code: have Claude write a Three.js scene, render it headlessly in a browser, and capture it frame by frame into video, instead of paying an AI video model or a motion designer.
tactics.mechanism: A browser renders a 3D code scene the way a high-end website does, and a screenshot at 60fps turns it into frames. Generation costs only text tokens (~37K tokens, about 5 cents on a subscription for a 15-second clip). Every revision is a cheap code edit, whereas a video model charges per second (~$1.50 per 15 seconds) and charges again for each change.
tactics.evidence: Five on-screen demos, and the creator says this is how all motion graphics in the video itself were made. The token arithmetic is shown for one clip, compared against Seedance 2.5 per-second pricing. He uses it daily on his own channel.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC posts organic video to Instagram and Facebook every day. Its core claims are non-demonstrable mechanism claims (what aluminium-free means, how odour forms, what is actually in the bar or cream), which the product-image-stack skill says need 'a different home' than a frame. A code-rendered animated explainer is that home. The first surface is Reels: a 3D ingredient breakdown or a 'how your deodorant works' piece, with the spoken or on-screen hook carrying the claim. It can also be cut as a 5-10 second mechanism beat between Trybe UGC lines. The same render can then be recommended to David Parrotino as a Meta creative variant and used as a Shopify PDP gallery or Amazon video asset. One person with a Claude subscription runs this end to end today, at near-zero marginal cost, so it is unstaged. The score is not higher because RSC's brand register is natural and believable, so the glossy glassmorphic and metallic look shown must be restyled toward the brand palette or it will read as an ad. The paid-creative skill also treats 'attractive' as a failure mode in native formats. Any depicted mechanism must stay inside what the formula substantiates.

tactics.claim: Write the motion-graphics prompt as a scene-by-scene spec: say what happens in each scene and when, name Three.js as the framework, call for shaders where appropriate, and name the visual treatment (e.g. glassmorphic frosted panes).
tactics.mechanism: The model builds exactly what it is told. Specific per-scene timings remove ambiguity. Naming Three.js unlocks 3D rather than Claude's default flat 2D graphics. Naming shaders unlocks GPU effects (reflections, glows, particles) that create the premium feel. A capable model decides where shaders belong once permitted.
tactics.evidence: The demo prompts are shown on screen beside their outputs. He contrasts them with 'those flat motion graphics which Claude usually creates'.

rscFit.reasoning: This is the operating spec for the code-render tactic above, applied to RSC explainers. Example scene list: 0-2s spoken hook plus on-screen text, 2-6s a 3D molecule of the ingredient, 6-10s camera move to the product pack, 10-15s CTA. It is runnable today by one person. It is distinct from the existing scene-type menu, which covers which kind of cutaway fits a script segment, not how to instruct a 3D code renderer. The visual-treatment line should name RSC's own palette and texture (hex codes, natural or paper textures, like his fourth demo) rather than the tech-glass look, to stay on brand.
